title: Chapter 115 — The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
paragraphs: And jolly enough they were, the sights and sounds that came sweeping down before the wind a few weeks after Ahab's harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just squeezed in her last cask of oil and bolted down her bulging hatches. Now, decked out in cheerful holiday finery, she was sailing joyfully — if a little boastfully — around among the widely scattered ships on the cruising ground before turning her prow for home.

The three men at her mastheads wore long streamers of narrow red bunting on their hats; from the stern a whaleboat was hung, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was the long lower jaw of the last whale they had killed. Signals, ensigns and jacks of all colors were flying from her rigging on every side. Lashed sideways in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above them, in her topmast crosstrees, you saw slender breakers (small casks) of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast, was a brass lamp.

It was learned afterward that the Bachelor had had the most astonishing success — all the more remarkable because many other ships cruising the same seas had gone whole months without taking a single fish. She had not only given away barrels of beef and bread to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but had also traded for extra casks from the ships she met, and these were stowed along the deck and in the captain's and officers' staterooms. Even the cabin table had been broken up for kindling, and those who ate in the cabin took their meals off the broad head of an oil-butt lashed to the floor as a centerpiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and tarred their sea chests and filled them. It was added, as a joke, that the cook had fitted a lid on his largest boiler and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooners had capped the sockets of their irons and filled them; that in fact everything was filled with sperm except the captain's trouser pockets, and those he kept free to thrust his hands into, as smug evidence of his complete satisfaction.

As this happy ship of good fortune bore down on the gloomy Pequod, the barbaric boom of enormous drums came from her forecastle. As she came closer still, a crowd of her men could be seen standing around her huge try-pots, which had been covered with the parchment-like poke, or stomach skin, of the black fish, and which roared loudly at every blow of the crew's clenched fists. On the quarter-deck the mates and harpooners were dancing with the olive-skinned girls who had run off with them from the Polynesian Isles, while three Long Island negroes, perched in a decorated boat hung high and firmly secured between the foremast and mainmast, led the riotous jig with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory. Meanwhile others of the crew were noisily busy tearing apart the brickwork of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been taken out. You would almost have thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they let out as the now useless brick and mortar went hurtling into the sea.

Lord and master of the whole scene, the captain stood upright on the ship's raised quarter-deck, where the entire joyful spectacle played out in full view before him, and seemed to have been staged solely for his own amusement.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other's wakes — one all celebrations for things past, the other all forebodings for things to come — their two captains in themselves embodied the whole striking contrast of the scene.
"Come aboard, come aboard!" cried the gay Bachelor's commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" gritted Ahab in reply.
"No; only heard of him; but don't believe in him at all," said the other good-humoredly. "Come aboard!"
"You are too damned jolly. Sail on. Have you lost any men?"

"Not enough to speak of — two islanders, that's all; but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I'll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will you — merry's the play — a full ship and homeward-bound."

"How wondrously familiar a fool is!" muttered Ahab; then aloud: "You are a full ship and homeward-bound, you say; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go your ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

So, while one ship ran cheerfully before the breeze, the other fought stubbornly against it, and the two vessels parted. The Pequod's crew watched the retreating Bachelor with grave, lingering looks, but the Bachelor's men, caught up in their lively celebration, paid no attention to their gaze. And as Ahab leaned over the taffrail and watched the homeward-bound ship, he took a small vial of sand from his pocket; then, looking from the ship to the vial, he seemed to be bringing two distant associations together, for that vial held Nantucket soundings.
